note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Cut bend and install electrical conduits

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: You lead a team of three putting steel conduit into a new classroom block in Old Harbour. What should you do before anyone cuts conduit?
options: Order half as much again, so the team never runs short
Check the drawings on site, agree routes and brief the team
Let each person choose a route, so the work goes faster
Bend the longest runs first, so the hard work is done early

questions.stem: The drawing shows a conduit run passing straight through a steel roof beam. What should the team leader do?
options: Drill through the beam, because the drawing shows the route
Cut a notch in the edge of the beam for the conduit to sit in
Weld a bracket to the beam and carry on without asking
Stop, report the clash and agree a new route in writing

questions.stem: Which conduit is the best choice for runs on the open roof of a hotel in Negril, close to the sea and in full sun?
options: Thin-wall steel tubing with set-screw couplings
Black enamelled steel conduit with mild steel saddles
UV-resistant PVC conduit with non-rusting fixings
Flexible metal conduit laid loose along the roof

questions.stem: A motor sits on a slide base that moves to tighten its belt. How should the conduit be taken into the motor's terminal box?
options: With a rigid steel bend screwed tight into the box
With a short length of flexible conduit and glands
With PVC conduit cemented into the box entry
With bare cable clipped from the conduit end

questions.stem: Your team must extend conduit from an existing box that holds a working 110 V circuit. What must happen before the box lid comes off?
options: Switch off at the outlet and work quickly
Wear rubber gloves so the circuit can stay on
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove it dead
Ask the customer to keep away while you work

questions.stem: During safe isolation, the tester shows no voltage at the box. Afterwards it gives no reading on the proving unit either. What does this mean?
options: The circuit is dead and work on it can start now
The proving unit is faulty and must be binned
The circuit is live and the breaker is faulty
The result is unsafe; retest with a good tester

questions.stem: A trainee is warming PVC conduit with a heat gun next to open tins of solvent cement. What should you, as team leader, tell him?
options: Move the heating well away from the cement and its fumes
Hold the gun closer, so each bend is done more quickly
Carry on, because solvent cement does not burn easily
Point the gun at the floor between bends to cool it down

questions.stem: The team must cut chases in block walls for concealed conduit. Which is the best control for the dust?
options: Sweep the dust up dry once the whole job is finished
Wet the wall first and keep the windows shut
Wear a paper mask and ask others to stay outside
Use a wall chaser with extraction, plus masks and goggles

questions.stem: Conduit must be fixed along a workshop ceiling 4.5 m high. Which access is best for this job?
options: A stepladder standing on top of a workbench
A ladder leaned against the conduit run
A mobile tower, put up and checked correctly
A chair standing on a scaffold board on trestles

questions.stem: An offset 150 mm deep is made with two 45° bends. The multiplier for 45° is about 1.4. How far apart are the two bend marks?
options: 105 mm
150 mm
210 mm
300 mm

questions.stem: An offset with two 30° bends is 150 mm deep. For 30° bends the run gets shorter by about 0.27 × the depth (the shrink). About how much shorter is the run?
options: 15 mm
27 mm
75 mm
40 mm

questions.stem: A long run already has several bends. Why might you make a deep offset with two 22½° bends instead of two 45° bends?
options: Smaller bends always need fewer saddles
They add less total bending to the run
They make the offset shorter along the wall
They mean the conduit end need not be reamed

questions.stem: The bender maker's chart gives a take-up of 150 mm for 20 mm conduit. A 90° stub must rise 500 mm from the end of the conduit. Where is the bend mark?
options: 150 mm from the end
350 mm from the end
500 mm from the end
650 mm from the end

questions.stem: A specification lets cables fill 40% of a conduit's inside area. The inside area is 320 mm² and each cable takes up 16 mm². What is the most cables allowed?
PVC conduit grows about 0.06 mm per metre for each 1 °C it warms. A 25 m run on a roof warms by 30 °C in the sun. About how much longer does it get?
options: 45 mm
4.5 mm
75 mm
450 mm

questions.stem: A run between two draw-in boxes already has three 90° bends. The specification allows 360° of bending between draw-in points. The route needs two more 90° bends. What is the best plan?
options: Make both bends and use extra cable lubricant
Make both bends tighter so they take less room
Add a draw-in box so each part stays within the limit
Leave out some saddles so the cables pull more freely

questions.stem: A straight steel run is made from 14 full lengths of conduit, joined end to end. How many couplings join them?
Why does a steel conduit end cut with a wheel pipe cutter usually need more reaming than one cut with a hacksaw?
options: The cutter leaves the end badly out of square
The cutter rolls a bigger burr into the bore
The cutter strips the zinc from the outside
The cutter makes the thread harder to start

questions.stem: How long should the thread be on a steel conduit end that screws into a coupling?
options: As long as possible, so it screws further into the coupling
Half the coupling length, to save time
Enough for the two ends to butt inside the coupling
Any length, because paint will cover it

questions.stem: A trainee's thread on heavy-gauge conduit is torn and rough. What is the most likely cause?
options: The conduit was held in a pipe vice
The die was turned back now and then
The conduit was reamed before threading
The die was blunt or no cutting oil was used

questions.stem: Why should the welded seam of steel conduit be kept away from the outside of a bend?
options: It may split open as the outside stretches
It would scratch the former of the bender
It makes the finished bend come out too tight
It stops the conduit from being earthed

questions.stem: A job needs many bends in 25 mm heavy-gauge steel conduit. Which equipment is best for the bending?
options: A bending spring pushed into the steel tube
A heat gun to warm the steel until it bends
A bench vice and a hammer to work it round
A bending machine with the right former and guide

questions.stem: After the second bend is made, a length of conduit rocks and will not lie flat on the wall. What caused this?
options: The conduit was cut too long before it was bent
The maker's take-up figure was used for the mark
The conduit was reamed before it was bent
The second bend was twisted out of line with the first

questions.stem: Why must a heated PVC bend be held in shape until it has cooled?
options: So the cement on the coupling sets at the same time
So its colour does not fade later in the sun
So the PVC sets in shape and does not spring back
So the conduit can be threaded while it is soft

questions.stem: Which bend angles are commonly used for a three-bend saddle over a small pipe?
options: 90° in the middle and 45° each side
30° in the middle and 60° each side
22½° in the middle and 45° each side
45° in the middle and 22½° each side

questions.stem: A 90° bend has a centre-line radius of 100 mm. About how long is the curved part of the conduit (a quarter of a circle)?
options: 157 mm
100 mm
200 mm
314 mm

questions.stem: Why does the spacing of conduit supports come from the maker's tables or the specification, and not from guesswork?
options: Fewer saddles always look neater on the wall
Spacing depends on conduit type, size and position
Saddles must be the same distance apart in every job
Guessing is only a problem for steel conduit

questions.stem: Steel conduit must be fixed to a timber roof truss in a house in Mandeville. Which fixing is right?
options: Saddles held with wood screws of the right size
Saddles held with masonry nails driven at an angle
Wall plugs pushed into holes in the timber
Cable ties around the truss and the conduit

questions.stem: How should a long, straight PVC run in the sun be fixed so it can grow and shrink?
options: Cement every joint and screw every saddle down hard
Fit expansion couplings and saddles that let it slide
Use steel couplings in place of PVC ones
Paint the conduit black so it stays cooler

questions.stem: A steel conduit run outdoors goes down a wall and into a box at the bottom. What should be done about water that condenses inside?
options: Seal every joint and leave the water inside
Fill the conduit with grease so water cannot enter
Fit a drain at the low point and avoid water traps
Drill holes along the top of the run to let air in

questions.stem: A conduit must pass through a fire-rated wall between a kitchen and a store. What must be done after it is fixed?
options: Leave the gap open so air can move through
Fill the gap with paper and paint over it
Seal the gap with an approved fire-stopping product
Fill the gap with foam made for draught-proofing

questions.stem: Data cables and 110 V power cables are planned for the same route. What is good practice?
options: Put them in separate conduits, kept apart as specified
Pull them into one conduit to save on material
Tape the data cables to the outside of the conduit
Use the power conduit and wrap data cables in tape

questions.stem: Two fixed lengths of steel conduit, already saddled, must be joined in the middle and neither can be turned. Which fitting is used?
options: A conduit union or split coupling
A standard coupling screwed on tight
A PVC adaptor cemented in place
A cable tie wrapped around both ends

questions.stem: A steel conduit run will be part of the earth path. A trainee has painted the threads before screwing them into the boxes. What is the risk?
options: The paint will make the threads rust more quickly
The paint may break the earth path at the joints
The paint will make the conduit too hot to touch
The paint will stop the cables being drawn in

questions.stem: A continuity test on a long steel conduit run gives a much higher reading than the other runs. What should the team leader check first?
options: Whether the run is painted in the right colour
Whether the saddles are spaced too closely
Whether a coupling, locknut or connector is loose
Whether the cables in the run are too small

questions.stem: Before cables are drawn in, why do you pull a brush or swab through each finished conduit run?
options: To polish the inside so it does not rust
To check the earth path at each coupling
To clear out water, grit and swarf
To measure the exact length of the run

questions.stem: When drawing several cables into a long run, why is one person kept at the feed end?
options: To count how many metres are pulled through
To feed the cables in straight and stop any twisting
To push the cables so the puller needs no help
To cut each cable to length as it goes in

questions.stem: You check a trainee's saddle bend and find the outside of the middle bend is flattened. What is the best response as team leader?
options: Accept it, because cables can still be drawn through
Fill the flat with paint so it cannot be seen
Have it remade, and show him how to avoid the fault
Fit an extra saddle over the flat part to hide it

questions.stem: Which is the best way to check that a long horizontal run is level along its whole length?
options: Judge it by eye from one end of the room
Measure up from the floor at one end only
Use a laser level or a long level at many points
Count the saddles and check they are equal

questions.stem: Part of a conduit route was moved on site to clear a water pipe. What must the team leader do about it?
options: Nothing, as long as the cables reach the boxes
Mark the change on the drawing for the as-built record
Tell the plumber, who keeps the electrical drawings
Paint the moved part of the run a different colour

questions.stem: Which items belong in the completion report you hand over for a conduit installation?
options: Only the names of the people who did the work
Routes, changes, test results and open snags
A list of the tools that were used on the job
The time each member arrived and left each day

questions.stem: Which conduit is the best choice for a run cast into a concrete floor slab?
options: Heavy-gauge conduit made for use in concrete
Thin-wall flexible conduit with no couplings
Plastic garden hose with the ends taped up
Light-gauge PVC trunking with clip-on lids

questions.stem: Why should steel conduit, boxes and fittings in one system all be of the same finish, such as all galvanised?
options: Mixed finishes make the conduit heavier to carry
Galvanised fittings cannot be threaded at all
Different finishes stop cables being drawn in
Mixed metals can corrode each other at the joints

questions.stem: At the end of each day on site, what should the team leader make sure happens?
options: Off-cuts cleared, tools stored, open ends capped
All saddles removed so the run can be checked tomorrow
Every tin of cement left open so it does not set
The bender left at the work face for the morning

questions.stem: When is a heat gun or heating box a better choice than a bending spring for PVC conduit?
options: For every bend, because heat is always quicker
For short bends close to the end of a length
For larger sizes and sets the spring cannot make
For conduit that will be buried in concrete

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A shallow step of 60 mm uses two 22½° bends, with a multiplier of 2.6. Give the gap between the bend marks in millimetres.
What is the offset multiplier for two 60° bends, to one decimal place?
What two-word name is given to the part of a conduit's inside area that the cables fill, given as a percentage?
A conduit has an inside area of 450 mm². Cables may fill 40% of it. Each cable takes up 18 mm². How many cables are allowed?
PVC conduit grows about 0.06 mm per metre for each 1 °C rise. By how many millimetres does a 40 m run grow when it warms by 25 °C?
A 90° bend has a centre-line radius of 140 mm. Using π = 3.14, how long is the curved part of the bend, to the nearest millimetre?
A bender's take-up for 25 mm conduit is 125 mm. A stub must rise 400 mm. How far from the end of the conduit, in millimetres, is the bend mark?
A run has bends of 90°, 45°, 45° and 90° between two draw-in boxes. What is the total bending, in degrees?
Pieces 650 mm long are cut from one 3 m length of conduit. Ignoring the saw cuts, how many whole pieces can be cut?
What is the name of the zinc coating put on steel conduit by dipping it in molten zinc?
What is the name of the fitting with a removable lid put part-way along a long run so that cables can be pulled in in stages?
What is the name of the work of sealing the gap round a conduit where it passes through a fire-rated wall or floor?
What is put on cables to cut friction when they are pulled into a conduit? Give its usual name.
What two letters begin the code, such as 65, that shows how well a box or fitting keeps out dust and water?
What fitting is put at the lowest point of an outdoor steel conduit run to let condensed water out?

essays.stem: You lead a team that will install surface steel conduit in a small shop in Spanish Town: a board, six outlets and four lights. Explain how you would plan the work before the first length is cut.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first read the drawings, the specification and the work order, and check which conduit type, sizes and finish are asked for. Then I would walk the site with the drawing to confirm the routes, box positions and heights, and look for clashes with beams, pipes, doors and other trades. I would check that no run needs too much bending between draw-in points and add draw-in boxes where needed. I would do a take-off of conduit, bends, boxes, saddles and fixings, with an allowance for waste, and order early. I would do a risk assessment covering ladders or towers, dust, power tools and any existing circuits, and plan safe isolation where we connect to them. Last, I would set the order of work, give each member clear tasks, and agree the plan with my supervisor and the shop owner.
markingPoints: Reads drawings, specification and work order; confirms conduit type, size and finish
Site visit: confirms routes, box positions and heights, and finds clashes
Plans draw-in points and limits bending between them
Makes a take-off with a waste allowance and orders materials in time
Risk assessment (access, dust, tools, safe isolation), task allocation and approval of the plan

essays.stem: A conduit on a wall must step out by 100 mm to clear a beam. Explain how you would work out and mark an offset using two 30° bends, including the effect of shrink. Show the figures.
essays.modelAnswer: An offset is two equal bends in opposite directions that move the run sideways by the depth needed. For 30° bends the multiplier is 2, so the distance between the two bend marks is 100 mm × 2 = 200 mm. Making the offset also uses up some length, called shrink. For 30° bends the shrink is about 0.27 × the depth, so 100 × 0.27 = about 27 mm. I would measure from a fixed point, such as the box, to where the offset must be complete, then add the shrink to that distance so the run still ends in the right place. I would mark the first bend, then the second bend 200 mm further along, both on the same side of the conduit. I would make the first bend to 30°, turn the conduit through exactly half a turn, line up the second mark and make the second bend, then check the depth and that both legs are parallel and not twisted.
markingPoints: Distance between marks = depth × multiplier: 100 × 2 = 200 mm
Explains shrink and works it out (about 27 mm) and allows for it
Measures from a fixed point and marks both bends in line
Turns the conduit half a turn for the second bend so the bends are opposite and not twisted
Checks the finished depth and that the legs are parallel

essays.stem: Explain how a steel conduit system can be part of the earth path, what can make that path fail, and how you would test and record it.
essays.modelAnswer: When the specification allows it, steel conduit, boxes and fittings can carry earth fault current back to the board, so the joints must be good conductors. Each length must be screwed fully into couplings and boxes, with the ends meeting, and every locknut and connector tight on clean metal. The path can fail if joints are loose, if threads or box entries are painted or rusty, if a length has a cracked weld or is damaged, or if a PVC part has been put into the run. Many specifications also ask for a separate earth conductor in the conduit as well. To test, the run must be dead with no supply connected. I would use a low-resistance ohmmeter, null the leads first, and measure from the earth terminal at the board to each box. Any reading much higher than the others shows a poor joint to find and fix. I would write each reading on the test record with the date and my name.
markingPoints: Conduit and fittings carry fault current, so every joint must conduct well
Names causes of failure: loose joints, paint or rust, damage, a PVC part in the run
Tests dead, with a low-resistance ohmmeter and leads nulled
Compares readings from the board to each box and follows up high readings
Records each result with date and name (mentions a separate earth conductor where specified)

essays.stem: Explain why the number of cables in a conduit and the amount of bending between draw-in points must be limited. Then show how you would check whether eight cables can go into one conduit.
essays.modelAnswer: Too many cables in a conduit makes them hard to pull in, so the insulation can be scraped or stretched, and packed cables cannot lose heat, so they may overheat in use. Too much bending between draw-in points adds friction at every bend, so the pull gets very hard and cables can be damaged. Specifications therefore limit the fill and the total degrees of bending, and draw-in boxes are added to split long or bent runs. To check eight cables, I would find the inside area of the conduit from the maker's data, for example 320 mm², and the area of one cable over its insulation, for example 16 mm². If the specification allows 40% fill, the space allowed is 0.4 × 320 = 128 mm². Eight cables take 8 × 16 = 128 mm², so eight just fit. If they did not fit, I would use a larger conduit or split the circuits.
markingPoints: Overfilling: damage when pulling in, and overheating in use
Bending adds friction; limit total bending and add draw-in boxes
Uses inside area from maker's data and cable area over insulation
Works out the allowed area from the fill percentage and compares it with the total cable area
Says what to do if the cables do not fit (bigger conduit or split runs)

essays.stem: A 30 m PVC conduit run will be fixed along the outside wall of a factory in St Catherine, in full sun. Explain why expansion matters and how you would allow for it.
essays.modelAnswer: PVC grows much more with heat than steel does. In the Jamaican sun an outside wall can warm the conduit by 30 °C or more between night and midday. If PVC grows about 0.06 mm per metre for each degree, a 30 m run warming by 30 °C grows about 0.06 × 30 × 30 = 54 mm. If the run is fixed hard at both ends, this growth makes it bow out between saddles, pull out of boxes or crack joints. To allow for it, I would fit expansion couplings at the spacing the maker gives, set to the right opening for the temperature on the day. I would use saddles that let the conduit slide, and fix it hard only where the maker says. I would also use a UV-resistant grade and seal outdoor boxes so water cannot get in.
markingPoints: PVC expands much more than steel; sun heats the run
Works out the growth with a sum (about 54 mm for the example)
Effects if not allowed for: bowing, joints pulling apart or cracking
Expansion couplings at the maker's spacing, set for the day's temperature
Saddles that let it slide; UV-resistant grade and weatherproof boxes

essays.stem: As team leader, describe how you would check the conduit work of two trainees during a job, which faults you would look for, and how you would deal with them.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check their work at stages, not only at the end, so faults are found before the run is fixed and hard to change. At the cutting stage I would look for square cuts, and ends reamed smooth with no burr inside. On threads I would check the length, that the thread is clean and not torn, and that bare thread is protected. On bends I would look for flattening, kinks or wrinkles, bends twisted out of line, wrong angles or offsets that do not match the depth. On fixing I would check saddle spacing, saddles near boxes and bends, runs level and plumb, and tight couplings and box connections. When I found a fault I would show the trainee what was wrong and why it matters, have it put right or remade, and check it again. I would note repeated faults so more training can be given.
markingPoints: Checks at stages during the job, not only at the end
Cutting and threading faults: square cut, burrs, thread length and condition
Bending faults: flattening, kinks, twist, wrong angle or depth
Fixing faults: saddle spacing and positions, level and plumb, tight joints
Explains, has it remade, re-checks and records for further training

essays.stem: Describe how you would organise your team to draw five cables into a finished conduit run that has three bends and one draw-in box.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check that the run is complete, fixed and clean: I would pull a brush or swab through to clear water and grit, and check that bushes are fitted so there are no sharp edges. I would check the cable sizes and colours against the circuit schedule and that the fill is within the limit. The cable drums would be set up on a stand at the feed end so they turn freely and the cables do not twist. I would push a fish tape or draw wire through to the draw-in box and attach the cables to it in a neat, tapered bundle, taped firmly. One person feeds the cables in straight and uses cable lubricant if needed, while another pulls steadily at the draw-in box. We would talk to each other the whole time and stop if the pull gets hard. Then we repeat for the next section, leave enough cable at each box, and label the ends.
markingPoints: Checks the run first: complete, swabbed clean, bushes fitted, fill within limit
Drums on a stand so cables run freely without twisting
Fish tape or draw wire, with cables taped in a neat tapered bundle
One feeds and one pulls steadily, with lubricant if needed; uses the draw-in box to pull in stages
Clear communication; leaves enough cable and labels the ends

essays.stem: Your team will install conduit at ceiling height in a busy office in Kingston, close to circuits that are in use. Describe the hazards and the controls you would put in your risk assessment.
essays.modelAnswer: Working at height is a main hazard, so I would use a mobile tower or podium steps that are checked and set up correctly, with the wheels locked, and keep people from walking under the work. Existing circuits are a shock hazard. Before we drill near them or open any box, the circuit would be isolated, locked off with our own lock, tagged, and proved dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. I would use a cable and pipe detector before drilling. Drilling block and concrete makes dust and noise, so I would use extraction, masks, goggles and ear protection, and work at agreed times. Tools and off-cuts can fall or trip people, so I would cordon the area and keep it tidy. Office staff must be told about power cuts in advance. Every member would be briefed before work starts.
markingPoints: Work at height: suitable checked platform, wheels locked, area below kept clear
Existing circuits: full safe isolation with the tester checked before and after
Detector before drilling; dust and noise controls with PPE
Cordon and housekeeping to protect office staff
Tells staff about power cuts and briefs the team

essays.stem: Explain how the Jamaican climate and a site close to the sea affect your choice and installation of conduit systems. Give examples.
essays.modelAnswer: Salt air near the sea makes steel rust fast, so I would choose PVC conduit, or steel with a heavy galvanised or other protective finish where steel is needed for strength. Fixings should be stainless steel or plastic, and all parts of a steel system should have the same finish so they do not corrode each other. Any bare thread or cut must be painted with zinc-rich paint. Strong sun breaks down ordinary PVC, so outdoor PVC must be a UV-resistant grade, and its large expansion in the heat needs expansion couplings and saddles that let it slide. Heavy rain and humidity mean boxes and fittings need a suitable IP rating, entries from below where possible, drains at low points and no water traps. In hurricane areas, supports must be strong and closer together where the run is exposed to wind.
markingPoints: Salt air: PVC, or protected steel, with non-rusting fixings and matching finishes
Protects cut or bare steel (zinc-rich paint)
Sun: UV-resistant PVC and allowance for expansion
Rain and humidity: IP-rated boxes, drains, no water traps
Wind and storms: strong, well-spaced fixings on exposed runs

essays.stem: When a conduit installation is finished, describe the final checks you would make and the records you would hand to your supervisor.
essays.modelAnswer: I would walk every run with the drawing and check that all conduit is complete and fixed firmly, level and plumb, with saddles near every box and bend. I would check that all cuts are reamed, bushes and lids are fitted, spare knockouts are closed and outdoor fittings are sealed. I would check fire stopping where runs pass through fire-rated walls, and that runs are kept apart from other services as specified. For steel runs I would make sure the earth continuity test has been done dead and the results recorded. Any fault would go on a snag list with who will fix it and when. Then I would hand over a marked-up as-built drawing showing any route changes, the test record, the snag list, a note of materials used and returned, and a short report on progress and any problems.
markingPoints: Walks every run against the drawing: fixed, level, plumb, saddles in place
Checks finishing: reamed ends, bushes, lids, knockouts, weather sealing, fire stopping
Confirms continuity tests were done dead and recorded
Snag list with who fixes what and when
Hands over as-built drawing, test record, materials note and short report

practical1.title: Plan, install and test a steel conduit system feeding three boxes
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a drawing of a training bay with a distribution point and three steel boxes at different heights, with a beam or pipe that the run must clear. First, as a group, write a short plan: a take-off of conduit and fittings, the offset and saddle calculations (multiplier and shrink), where draw-in points go, the order of work, and who does what. Choose one member as team leader for each stage (planning, bending, fixing, testing) so that every member leads once and is checked by the others. Then install the system in steel conduit, with at least one 90° bend, one offset and one three-bend saddle. Every member cuts, reams and bends at least one length while the assessor watches; with heavy-gauge conduit, every member also cuts a thread. When it is finished, test the earth continuity of the run from the distribution point to each box with a low-resistance ohmmeter, with no supply anywhere on the bay, and write the results on a test record. Photograph each stage and hand in the plan, the calculation sheet and the test record with the photos.
materials: Drawing of the training bay from the assessor
Steel conduit (20 mm or as given), couplings, connectors, locknuts, bushes, steel boxes and saddles
Hand bender or bending machine to suit the conduit
Die stock with dies and cutting oil (for heavy-gauge conduit)
Hacksaw with a fine-tooth blade or pipe cutter, reamer and half-round file
Pipe vice, tape measure, marker, protractor or angle finder, spirit level
Hammer drill, masonry bit, wall plugs and screws, or the bay's fixing board
Low-resistance ohmmeter
Plan sheet, calculation sheet and test record form
Safety glasses, gloves, dust masks and ear protection
photos: The written plan and calculation sheet, with the stage leaders named
The run marked out on the bay, with bend and saddle positions
The offset and the three-bend saddle in place, with a level on them
The finished system, from the front, with all boxes connected
A close-up of one box entry, with locknut and bush
The continuity test being done, and the completed test record
The bay cleaned up, with off-cuts and swarf removed
checklist: Took part in the plan; the offset and shrink figures were worked out correctly
Led one stage clearly, giving tasks and checking the others' work
Measured, cut square and reamed at least one length (and cut a clean thread if heavy-gauge)
Made at least one bend to the right angle, without flattening or twist
Fixed conduit level and plumb, with saddles near boxes and bends
Made tight joints and box connections with locknuts and bushes
Carried out or checked the continuity test dead, and filled in the record correctly
Left the bay safe and tidy, with tools returned
safety: The bay has no supply connected at any time
Wear safety glasses when cutting, reaming, threading and drilling
Treat cut ends and swarf as sharp: wear gloves and clear swarf with a brush, not by hand
Keep cutting oil off the floor and wipe up spills at once
Check power tools and leads before use, and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Set out, install and inspect an outdoor-style PVC conduit system with expansion provision
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a sketch of a PVC conduit system for an outside wall: a long straight run (at least 4 m on the bay) with an expansion coupling, a draw-in box, a run that passes through a sleeve in a partition (to stand for a fire-rated wall), and two weatherproof boxes. As a group: (1) work out the expansion for the full run using the figure the assessor gives, and decide where the expansion coupling goes and how it is set; (2) write a short method statement and risk assessment; (3) install the system, making bends with a bending spring or heat gun as the assessor allows; (4) seal the sleeve with the fire-stopping product provided; (5) swab the run and pull in a draw cord; (6) inspect the work against a checklist that the group writes, and mark up an as-built sketch. Each member makes at least one bend and two cemented joints while the assessor watches, and each member inspects one part of another member's work and signs the checklist for it. No cables and no supply are used. Photograph each stage and hand in the method statement, the expansion sum, the inspection checklist and the as-built sketch.
materials: Sketch of the system and the expansion figure, from the assessor
UV-resistant PVC conduit, couplings, an expansion coupling, a draw-in box, two weatherproof boxes and glands
Saddles that allow the conduit to slide
Solvent cement and cleaner, made for PVC conduit
Bending spring, and a heat gun if the assessor allows it
Fine-tooth saw or PVC cutter, deburring tool, tape measure, level and chalk line
A partition with a sleeve, and a fire-stopping sealant (or a practice sealant from the assessor)
Swab or brush, and a draw cord
Method statement, risk assessment and checklist forms
Safety glasses, gloves and dust masks
photos: The expansion sum and the method statement
The run set out on the bay with a chalk line and saddle marks
A bend being made, and a cemented joint being pushed home
The expansion coupling fitted and set, with a tape measure showing the opening
The sleeve through the partition, sealed
The finished system, with the draw cord through it
The signed inspection checklist and the as-built sketch
checklist: Worked out the expansion correctly and set the coupling as planned
Cut square and deburred, and made sound cemented joints, fully home
Made a smooth bend with no flattening or kinking
Fixed saddles so the conduit can slide, with the run straight and level
Sealed the sleeve neatly with the fire-stopping product
Inspected another member's work fairly and recorded faults clearly
Used the solvent cement safely: lid on, good airflow, away from heat
Left the bay clean and returned unused materials
safety: Use solvent cement only with good airflow, keep the lid on, and keep it away from heat guns and sparks
Use the heat gun only if the assessor allows it; never point it at people or leave it on unattended
Wear gloves when using solvent cement and fire-stopping products, and follow the maker's instructions
Keep cords and off-cuts off the floor so nobody trips
